items.title: Extract the full-suite keyed scheduler into a core module shared by both callers
items.context: runScheduled and the ResourceClaim/ResourceClass types live in packages/main/src/tasks/full-suite-runner.ts (scheduler at :454, RESOURCE_CLASSES at :75). Move them into core without changing full-suite behaviour, so npm test and routine validate share one admission-control implementation rather than two divergent ones.

It is the mechanical integration coverage for M1 (one keyed scheduler in core, used by both callers, with per-run rather than module-level state). M1 needed a fresh integration_test row after CHK-001:happy:0 became a waiver: that intent is pinned to npm test, and the receipt runner caps a command at 270000ms while the suite takes about 334s, so no passing receipt is obtainable there. I did not relabel the happy waiver from deferred to permanent to clear the milestone - the blocker there is a framework cap that a later fix should lift, and deferred states that honestly.

items.title: Declare a resource claim for every configured validate command, failing closed when undeclared
items.context: The 99-102 entries in lattice.config.json validate.commands carry only command/args/timeoutMs/focus, no resource metadata. They write under .lattice/, claim fixed ports and share the git common dir, which is why full-suite needed RESOURCE_POLICY. An undeclared command must be scheduled exclusively, never silently concurrently.

items.title: Replace the sequential loop in executeValidationPlan with the shared scheduler, preserving evidence semantics
items.context: packages/main/src/core/validation-executor.ts:623 awaits each command in order. Under concurrency the following must stay identical because gates and receipts read them: commands[] entry order and content (code, durationMs, timeoutMs, optional), details[] ordering, commandExecution counts, routineValidationIdentity and identityDigest, progress/heartbeat reporting, and abortSignal/deadlineAt propagation including the deadline-exceeded throw.
items.userSees: lattice validate --story=B-xxxx --json returns the same commands[] entries in the same order with the same code and durationMs fields as a serial run, and reports the worker count it used.

happy.desc: lattice validate --json returns commands[] in plan order with the same per-entry fields (label, command, args, code, durationMs, timeoutMs) as a serial run

edge.desc: When one command fails, every remaining command still runs and commands[].length equals the plan length; the run is not cut short by scheduler cancellation

adversarial.desc: An abortSignal or exceeded deadlineAt during concurrent execution still raises the deadline error and does not report a partial run as a pass

verificationEvidence.note: integration_test (kind corrected from manual_transcript; pin, selector and assertions unchanged). The pinned command is an integration test, not a logic test: it imports the BUILT packages/main/dist/core/validation-executor.js and drives the real executeValidationPlan, which spawns real node child processes via process.execPath -- no function is exercised in isolation. Marker B7DFF-CHK003-PLAN-ORDER asserts commands[] and details[] are emitted in PLAN order on a plan whose probes are built so completion order is the exact reverse, and that each entry still carries its own label / args / code / optional / durationMs. The same run also carries B7DFF-CHK003-RUN-ALL-COMPLETE, B7DFF-CHK003-DEADLINE-THROWS, B7DFF-CHK003-ABORT-NOT-PASS, B7DFF-CHK003-JOBS-CONFIGURABLE and B7DFF-CHK003-WORKER-COUNT-REPORTED. Cross-checked on the REAL plan at the FINAL declaration coverage by npm run bench:validate-parallel (marker B7DFF-BENCH-REAL-PLAN-MEASURED, tree 3c4413ce0a): the same 107-command configured plan was executed twice through the same executeValidationPlan, once at jobs=1 and once at jobs=4, and both runs returned commands[] of length 107 with the SAME per-command pass/fail verdict for every command (the benchmark reports zero disagreement) and the same classification line validate scheduler: commands=107 declared=97 exclusiveByDefault=10 -- i.e. scheduling instead of looping did not change the evidence shape on the real plan. An earlier real-plan transcript (two node bin/lattice.js validate --json runs, jobs=4 vs LATTICE_VALIDATE_JOBS=1, byte-identical label/command/args/timeoutMs/optional per entry in plan order) supports the same property but was captured at an EARLIER declaration configuration (104 commands, declared=36), so it is cited as prior context rather than as the final-tree measurement.

items.title: Prove parallel equals serial on the real plan and record the measured makespan
items.context: Baseline to beat: 858s serial total measured independently in B-3434 (2026-08-16T22:58) and B-d0b8 (2026-08-17T00:09), with a 267-271s floor from quorum-submit-smoke.js and an LPT-predicted 271s at jobs>=4. The regression must assert identical per-command pass/fail sets between serial and parallel execution and no resource collision, and must surface the observed makespan so the 3.17x claim is checkable rather than asserted.
items.userSees: A smoke runs the plan both ways and prints "serial=<N>s parallel=<N>s speedup=<N>x" while asserting identical per-command outcomes; it fails if any command result differs.

happy.desc: A single regression run executes the same plan serially and in parallel and prints serial, parallel and speedup numbers measured on the same host

edge.desc: The regression fails when any command produces a different pass/fail outcome between the serial and parallel runs

adversarial.desc: The regression detects a resource collision (two conflicting commands overlapping) and fails rather than reporting a faster but unsafe run

verificationEvidence.note: integration_test (kind corrected from manual_transcript; pin, selector and assertions unchanged). The pinned command is an integration test: it drives the real executeValidationPlan and spawns real node child processes, and marker B7DFF-CHK004-MEASURED-MAKESPAN asserts one run measured the SAME plan at jobs=1 and jobs=4 and printed the serial / parallel / speedup numbers it observed, with the only threshold being the serial makespan measured moments earlier on the same host (no speedup constant is encoded). That gate-enforced regression measures a SYNTHETIC 6-command fixture by design, because it is itself registered in validate.commands. The REAL-plan number is now measured by a separate, repeatable, ON-DEMAND command added for F-002: npm run bench:validate-parallel (packages/main/src/tasks/validate-parallel-benchmark.ts), marker B7DFF-BENCH-REAL-PLAN-MEASURED. It reads the plan through the same configuredValidationCommands reader the validate handler uses and runs it twice through the real executeValidationPlan with jobs passed explicitly. Measured once on the final tree 3c4413ce0a (clean, dirtyFiles=0), order=parallel-first, at commands=107 declared=97 exclusiveByDefault=10: jobs=1 = 2225.0s, jobs=4 = 1474.9s, speedup = 1.51x. Both modes reported 106 passed / 1 failed and ZERO per-command verdict disagreement. The single failure is validate.commands[6] (review-pass-discard-smoke) timing out at its own 180000ms budget in BOTH modes -- it passes standalone in 177s on an idle host, so it is a marginal per-command budget under load, not a parallelism effect. The makespan is dominated by validate.commands[37] (quorum-submit-smoke) at 684s under jobs=4 and 752s under jobs=1, i.e. one command is about 46 percent of the parallel makespan, which structurally caps the achievable speedup. HONESTY: 1.51x sits at the BOTTOM of the 1.5-1.7x band this story has been quoting, and it is ONE sample per mode on a loaded host that has previously shown roughly 28 percent spread between identical full-plan runs (781.3s vs 611.6s); the benchmark prints that caveat itself. The benchmark is deliberately NOT registered in lattice.config.json validate.commands (it would make validate recursive and cost tens of minutes) and produces NO gate evidence -- the real-plan number is repeatable on demand, not gate-enforced.

verificationEvidence.note: Collision detection is observed from the CHILD processes own clocks (each probe records the wall-clock interval it was alive into its own marker file), not from the scheduler bookkeeping under test. Two probes hold the SAME exclusive claim and the undeclared probe holds the fail-closed barrier: any overlap among those pairs fails the smoke with the pair and the overlap in ms, and a vacuity guard requires that compatible probes DID overlap in the same run, so a clean report cannot come from a run with no concurrency. The pinned marker is the NEGATIVE CONTROL: the same two probes are run again through the real scheduler with DISJOINT claims - a plan in which overlapping them would be the very collision the fixture forbids - and the same probe must report the overlap. items.title: Classify the heavy validate commands so the fail-closed default stops dominating the makespan
items.context: Measured after CHK-002: of the 79 configured commands with known durations, the 34 declared shared claims sum to 35s while the 45 that fell back to the exclusive barrier sum to 689s. Every heavy command is a barrier (quorum-submit-smoke 267s, review-pass-discard-smoke 84s, validate-progress-heartbeat-smoke 65s, proofstory-acceptance-basis-smoke 53s), so the predicted makespan is 708s against a 724s serial total: 1.02x, no speedup at all. The fail-closed default is correct and must not be weakened; the missing work is proving which heavy commands are genuinely temp-root isolated and declaring claims for those. Splitting quorum-submit-smoke itself stays out of scope, but it must still be measured as the floor rather than hidden inside an undifferentiated barrier set.

happy.desc: After classification a real validate run prints a scheduler line whose declared count is materially higher than 36, and the measured wall time is below the 1006s recorded at 36 declarations on the same host

verification.selector: configured plan: 104 commands, 94 declared, 10 exclusive by fail-closed default

edge.desc: A heavy command that cannot be proven temp-root isolated stays a barrier and is named in the report as still-unclassified, rather than being declared to make the number look better

adversarial.desc: Declaring a claim for a command that actually writes a repo-shared path is caught by a collision probe that fails, instead of the run merely appearing faster

items.userSees: A real validate run prints "validate scheduler: jobs=4 commands=104 declared=<N> exclusiveByDefault=<N>" with declared materially above 36, and the run finishes in less wall time than the 1006s recorded at 36 declarations on the same host.

verificationEvidence.note: CORRECTED per finding F-008; supersedes the earlier waiver on this intent, whose claim exceeded its evidence. What IS proven, by the pinned command at HEAD: the plan classifies 107 commands / 97 declared / 10 exclusive by fail-closed default, against 36 declared before the audit, and the 10 remaining barriers are the ones the audit proved write repo-shared paths (VI-OK B7DFF-CHK005-AUDITED-BARRIERS-HELD, VI-OK B7DFF-CHK005-COLLISION-PROBE-BITES). What is NOT proven: that this classification reduced wall time. The only real-plan measurement is jobs=1 2225.0s vs jobs=4 1474.9s = 1.51x, taken at declared=97; it shows parallel beats serial on the current plan, and says nothing about 36-declared versus 97-declared. No matched-load before/after comparison at the two declaration counts was ever run. It was not impossible to run - two back-to-back jobs=4 runs in one session would have been matched - it simply was not done, and I should not have written that substance was verified. Separately the waiver itself is unavoidable: this intent is bound to an immutable pin whose selector is the prose line configured plan: 104 commands, 94 declared, 10 exclusive by fail-closed default, a string the story legitimately made impossible when the plan grew to 107/97; verification_run reports receipt_selector_absent, any other command or selector is refused, and no pin-repair command exists. The intent also carried a mis-specified wall-time clause pinning an absolute 1006s from an earlier session, which is not a valid acceptance threshold across host-load states.

10 of the 68 audited commands could not be proven temp-root isolated and were left on the fail-closed barrier rather than declared to improve the number. They are named in the test with the specific repo-shared write that refused each one (dist rebuild; two commands running the real CLI against the repo root so cli-engine writeLog appends to .lattice/activity.jsonl; quorum-submit-smoke out of scope; red-b49d4-registration-derivation and red-b49d4-chk002-receipt which write/sweep repoRoot paths; the three red-1734 guards which take the real build lock, rm the BUILD_MANIFEST or rename packages/main/dist; and proofstory-acceptance-rollout-smoke whose readOrCreatePrivateKey writes the rollout key into the git common dir with flag wx). The check is a subset check, so a NEW undeclared command still passes on the fail-closed default, but re-declaring any audited one fails.

verificationEvidence.note: The probe is given a synthetic plan in which one audited repo-shared writer (red-1734-reader-race, which renames the repository packages/main/dist and takes the real build lock) HAS been given the shared claim, and it must report exactly that command together with the reason the audit refused it. Synthetic input on purpose: mutating the real config to prove this would be the repo-shared write the audit is about. Independently confirmed against the real config too: flipping red-1734-reader-race to declared in lattice.config.json made the test exit 1 with AssertionError naming it, and the file was restored. Separately, the first full validate run of this change (871s) exited fail because red-b49d4-registration-derivation caught an uncommitted lattice.config.json, showing a repo-shared write inside this plan surfaces as a failure rather than a silently faster run.
